one_liner: Embeddable C MessagePack codec; beat msgpack-c 1.1-3x in its author's 2016 suite; independent 2026 run: encode only.
what_it_does: MPack encodes and decodes MessagePack from C (also usable from C++), shipped as a two-file amalgamation (mpack.h, mpack.c) that you add to your build. It has three APIs: a Write API that encodes into a fixed buffer, a growable buffer or a flush callback (mpack_build_map/array can size compounds automatically); a Node API that parses a whole message into an immutable tree with DOM-style random access and key lookup; and an incremental Reader/Expect API with typed, range-checked reads. Errors are sticky: the first error puts the writer, reader or tree into an error state, later calls return safe zero/nil values, and you check once at destroy time. It is wire-compatible with msgpack-c but not an API drop-in (no msgpack_packer, msgpack_sbuffer or msgpack_object).
how_it_is_fast: Each write encodes straight into the writer's buffer: MPACK_WRITE_ENCODED checks the space left behind an MPACK_LIKELY branch, stores the big-endian bytes with __builtin_bswap helpers and only calls mpack_writer_ensure/flush when the 4096-byte buffer (MPACK_BUFFER_SIZE) fills. msgpack-c 1.3.0's C packer instead hands every element to a function pointer (msgpack_pack_append_buffer expands to (*user->callback)(...)), which plausibly explains why the C API trailed by 3.0x on small writes while msgpack's templated C++ packer trailed by only 1.3x (inference from the code, not profiled). The Node API parses iteratively with an explicit level stack rather than recursion, allocates node structs in 4 KB pages with each compound's children contiguous, points string and binary nodes into the source buffer without copying, and bounds allocation on hostile input by a 'possible nodes left' count (every element takes at least one byte).
when_to_use: Encoding MessagePack from C on a hot path: faster than msgpack-c in the author's 2016 suite (1.1-3.0x) and in the independent 2026 GLD.SerializerBenchmark run (1.15-1.68x against msgpack-c 6.0.1 across 10 workload groups, derived from its data).
Firmware and other constrained targets: no libc or allocator requirement, fixed buffers and node pools, builds for AVR/Arduino with 16-bit int and size_t, WebAssembly and inside the Linux kernel.
Parsing untrusted MessagePack into a random-access tree in C with one error check at the end, optional UTF-8 validation and message size and node-count limits (mpack_tree_set_limits).
Continuous streams such as RPC over a socket: mpack_tree_init_stream parses message after message, including non-blocking parsing.
Schema-known messages where the README recommends the Expect API for maximum speed and minimal memory (that path is not benchmarked anywhere read here).
when_not_to_use: Decode-heavy services already on current msgpack-c: in the 2026 GLD run (MPack 1.1.1 vs msgpack-c 6.0.1, gcc 11.4.0 -O2, i7-12800H) MPack's Node-API decode into structs was 1.03-1.35x slower in all 10 groups, and the round trip was a wash (MPack ahead in 5 groups, behind in 5).
JSON workloads: MessagePack only; the JSON siblings (yyjson-class parsers, json.cpp, cjson.cpp) are a different format.
C++ code that wants struct-level serialization from types or schemas: BitSerializer's MsgPack path, zpp::bits or protobuf-c generate that code, while MPack is a hand-written element-by-element API.

Reading untrusted data with the latest tagged release: v1.1.1 (2023-01-09) predates the August 2026 develop fixes for unbounded recursion in mpack_discard() (#126, stack overflow on deeply nested input), size_t overflow checks (#123, #124) and a range check in mpack_expect_*_alloc(); build from develop or backport.
Maps with many keys looked up by name: every mpack_node_map_cstr lookup scans all keys of the map to detect duplicates, so k lookups cost O(k*n).

integration.dependencies: none required; libc, stdio and malloc are optional and set by config macros (MPACK_STDLIB, MPACK_STDIO, MPACK_MALLOC); the repo's own build only runs the unit tests
integration.min_toolchain: C89/gnu89 (supported since v1.1), later C standards and C++; builds clean under /W4 with Visual Studio 2015-2019
integration.platforms: any: desktop and mobile OSes, WebAssembly, the Linux kernel (mpack-linux-kernel config), 8-bit AVR/Arduino; float and double can be disabled individually
integration.thread_safety: not documented; writers, readers and trees are caller-owned structs, so the natural pattern is one per thread

gotchas: Harness flaw in the cited suite: a fixed, separately measured hash time is subtracted from every row, which inflates ratios. Gross times give small-write 4.39 vs 8.68 us (1.98x, not 3.0x), small-tree 8.60 vs 10.08 us (1.17x, not 1.30x) and large-tree 767.61 vs 1104.32 us (1.44x, not 1.81x) against msgpack C (derived from page data). The 3.0x write headline mostly measures msgpack-c's callback-based C packer; msgpack's C++ packer is within 1.1-1.3x.

The 2016 numbers are for MPack 0.8.1 and msgpack-c 1.3.0 on GCC 5.3.0, and the harness uses the 0.8 API (mpack_tree_init parses immediately; 1.0 split it into init plus mpack_tree_parse), so the suite does not build against current MPack unchanged. The README's 'except CWPack' remark is not backed by the suite, which never ran CWPack.

The GLD comparison is not quite like for like on decode: its msgpack-c wrapper returns on the first matching key, while MPack's mpack_node_map_cstr_optional scans the whole map and flags duplicate keys as errors, so part of MPack's 1.03-1.35x decode deficit is extra validation.

Sticky errors mean a failed write or lookup silently returns 0/nil until you check mpack_writer_destroy() or mpack_tree_destroy(); element-count tracking for mpack_start_map/array is off in release builds (MPACK_READ_TRACKING and write tracking follow MPACK_DEBUG), so count mismatches are only caught in debug.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among catalogued C MessagePack options pick MPack over CMP whenever speed matters: in the same suite it wrote small data 3.4x faster (2.13 vs 7.33 us) and parsed incrementally 2.3x faster (3.20 vs 7.43 us), with CMP winning only on code size (3232 vs 4088 bytes). Prefer BitSerializer, zpp::bits or Cap'n Proto when you are in C++ and want type-driven serialization rather than an element-level C API.
verified_claims_summary: In ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks (written by MPack's author, 2016; GCC 5.3.0 -O3 -flto, AMD Phenom II X6 1090T, 7 runs of 10 s with best and worst dropped, hash time subtracted), MPack 0.8.1 encoded random schemaless data in 2.13 vs 6.42 us (msgpack C 1.3.0) and 2.77 us (msgpack C++) for a 2367-byte message and tree-parsed it in 4.99 vs 6.47 and 9.40 us, with matching output hashes. An independent 2026 run (GLD.SerializerBenchmark, MPack 1.1.1 vs msgpack-c 6.0.1, gcc 11.4.0 -O2, i7-12800H, about 90 trials per cell) confirms the encode lead (1.15-1.68x) but shows MPack's decode 1.03-1.35x slower in every group.
status_note: Active again on develop (fixes through 2026-08-08) but the last release is v1.1.1 from 2023-01-09, so security fixes for untrusted input are unreleased; MIT and two files, easy to vendor. The record's A-tier evidence is author-run on 2016 versions, and current independent data supports only the encode claim.
